World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: The community passionate about miniature versions of horses
World.content:
Maeve King "came out of the womb" obsessed with horses.

One of their clearest childhood memories was seeing figurines of the animal, about the size of a modern smartphone, at the shops.

It kickstarted a 25-year-long passion for model horses, which they now own hundreds of.

Maeve King has collected model horses since childhood. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

The Sydneysider is part of a worldwide community who collect and showcase intricate replicas of different horse breeds.

Hobbyists invest hundreds, and sometimes tens of thousands, of dollars in the process.

But to the untrained eye the "little plastic ponies" may appear as a simple plaything.

Riders and tack accompany model horses for a realistic diaroma. (Supplied: Kerri Afford)

"It's kind of a dichotomy of yes, they are just toys, and no, they can represent so much more," Ms King said.

"They are an avenue for community, for creativity … for self-expression, and for people to engage in horses in a way that can be cheaper than having an actual horse.

" I could not have 350 real-life horses in my apartment. "

'Just blows my mind'

Model horses can be made from plastic, resin, porcelain or 3D printed.

Each is handpainted meaning no two are the same.

Kerren Hampton has been collecting model horses for decades. (Supplied: Kerren Hampton)

Some are custom-order but the bulk are commercially sold straight out the box.

Traditional size is about 20cm tall, but can be as short as 7cm, with the pricepoint starting at about $60 per model.

Kerren Hampton was an early importer in the 90s, who would ship them around Australia via mail order.

She said nowadays, limited edition, vintage or special-run horses could fetch $10,000 or more.

While models can dip into the realm of fantasy, most are favoured for their realism — taking inspiration from famous horses.

"We even have ones after Australian horses like Winx and also Black Caviar … and many years ago, they did a model of [New Zealand-born] Phar Lap," long-term collector from South Australia, Kerri Afford said.

Hobbyists get together for live shows to present their collections and compete in different categories.

A selection of ribbons and vintage models. (Supplied: Kerri Afford) Each model horse is handpainted. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

A collection of horses in various stances at a live show. (Supplied: Kerri Afford)

Here, the models are accessorised with tack like saddles or reigns, and set up in realistic scenes accompanied by rider figurines.

They can be judged by the breed or colour class they are based on, and are separated by size.

"There are some that just blows my mind and you've got to look twice … because it looks so real," Ms Afford said.

Finding community down under

The community, spread out across the country, stay connected online.

Ms King said Australian collectors were close-knit and "everyone sort of knows each other".

Just some of Ms Afford's collection. (Supplied: Kerri Afford)

"It's a nice group of people who all have each other's backs and are overwhelmingly supportive and just have a really fun time in the face of what I think people often think is a really, really weird hobby," the 29-year-old said.

"I've experienced a lot of judgement before so it's nice being around other people who just sort of get it."

Ms Afford said the community was "quite big" with "thousands" involved nationwide.

Not everyone attends live shows but a "big" turnout could see dozens of participants, she said.

Meanwhile, a convention hosted by US manufacturer Breyer draws 30,000 attendees to Kentucky each year.

Loading...

"I don't know that we need to be as big as America or as crazy," Ms Afford said.

Ms Hampton said despite the larger population and deep "horse heritage" in the US, the same love was extended here.

"You've got your stockmen, your drovers and your light horseman, you've got your brumbies; there's still quite a horse culture in Australia," she said.

Beating misconceptions

This resin model has been "rehaired" with a mohair mane. (Supplied: Kerri Afford)

Ms Afford said there were always going to be people who thought collecting was for "nut cases".

"They think, 'What do you do? Do you gallop them around the table?'" she said.

"There are people out there that just want to ridicule what somebody does just because they don't understand it."

Kerri Afford says the model horse community is sizeable. (Supplied: Kerri Afford)

Despite this, Ms Afford said she saw new people discovering the hobby weekly — exacerbated recently by the Year of the Horse.

"I just see [the hobby] going forward and getting better.

" I myself don't plan on stopping collecting anytime soon. "

The horses have brought "a lot of joy" to Ms King. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

Ms King said the horses represented an "escape from reality".

"I think people would just dismiss it as silly and frivolous … and it kind of plays into the 'crazy horse girl' trope that exists.

"But this isn't hurting anyone and we're having a good time … it's brought a lot of joy to my life."

World.title: Regional sports 'stronger through diversity' as refugees thrive on field
World.content:
Amir Abdalla taps his hockey stick against the net posts twice and crouches in anticipation as the puck whizzes towards him.

He darts forward, and the puck bounces off his shin guards with a satisfying thwock.

"Good one, Amir!" comes the call from his teammates.

Amir Abdalla has been playing as goalkeeper for the Rangeville Hockey Club since March 2024. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

The 21-year-old goalie plays for the Rangeville Hockey Club in Toowoomba, 125 kilometres west of Brisbane.

"They're a part of my life now, and they're like family to me," Mr Abdalla said.

But Mr Abdalla's life has seen more turmoil than most on his hockey team.

He remembers in 2014, when he was just nine years old, fleeing his house in northern Iraq to escape ISIS, which was committing genocide on the Yazidi people.

"We had to run away from my house, my town, and go to the mountains," Mr Abdalla said.

"We stayed there for seven days with no food or water.

"All my family got kidnapped and killed on my father's side and my mother's side."

Mr Abdalla and his remaining family lived in abandoned buildings and refugee camps for years before they were approved to come to Australia as refugees in November 2022.

Hockey program for Yazidi community

Toowoomba has the highest number of Yazidi refugees in Australia.

Yazidis are a highly persecuted religious minority who predominantly come from Iraq, Turkey, Syria, and the Caucasus.

The community is dealing with the ongoing effects of enduring trauma while adjusting to life in regional Queensland.

Sport, hockey in particular, has been an outlet.

The Friday sessions at Toowoomba Hockey Club are run by volunteers. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Jessie McCartney runs Belong in Hockey, a Toowoomba Hockey Club program where every Friday morning, refugees learn to play hockey, have morning tea with the volunteers, and engage in educational sessions afterwards.

"We had a vision that sport can be the thing that helps these people get a sense of belonging in the community and improve their confidence and their language," Mr McCartney said.

Jessie McCartney runs the Belong in Hockey program in Toowoomba. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

He said since the program started in 2023, 140 refugees had participated in the program, including Mr Abdalla.

"We're very proud of Amir. He's become an advocate for hockey in the Yazidi community," Mr McCartney said.

In the three years that Mr Abdalla has been in Toowoomba, he has secured a full-time job as an air-conditioning and refrigeration apprentice and has recently bought a house.

Amir Abdalla is a Yazidi refugee from northern Iraq. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

"I always try to get better, like whatever it is in life," Mr Abdalla said.

Having graduated from the Belong in Hockey program in 2024, Mr Abdalla plays club hockey and volunteers on weekends, teaching children to play.

Sport 'stronger through diversity'

Hockey Australia has recognised the work of Belong in Hockey, and the Queensland government recently granted the program $95,000 to continue its services.

Mr McCartney has plans to expand the program to cater to other marginalised communities, including First Nations groups, people with disabilities, and veterans.

The volunteers and participants share morning tea after hockey training. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

He said Toowoomba was the ideal place to run this sort of program.

"We're 180,000 people, we're the second biggest inland city in Australia after Canberra, and we have an amazing sporting community," he said.

"Welcoming these people who have these amazingly diverse stories and histories and cultures helps make your sport a more enjoyable place for everyone."

About 20 participants attend the Belong in Hockey program on Friday mornings. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Chinar Ali, 19, has been playing on Friday mornings for three months.

She left Iraq with her siblings and came to Australia in 2024.

"It's very hard when you come to a different country and you don't know anything about it," Ms Ali said.

She said participating in Belong in Hockey had helped her to find her feet in Toowoomba.

Chinar Ali says hockey has helped her to make new friends and adapt to Australia. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

"They help us a lot, not just playing hockey but they help us how to make new friends, how to meet other people in different countries," she said.

"Because of [the program], we know what to do."

More than a game

Volunteer Erin Gilbar said she had "fallen in love" with the program and had since enlisted her parents to volunteer as well.

"The first session they [the participants] come along, [they're] a bit shy, don't have much English, but then over the course of a few months, suddenly they're one of the leaders," Ms Gilbar said.

" It's really heartwarming to see. "

She said she loved getting to know the Yazidi refugees and had even been invited to their homes for cultural celebrations.

Erin Gilbar volunteers at Belong in Hockey on Friday mornings. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Ms Gilbar said she felt she got "more out of it than the participants sometimes".

She was diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and had to stop playing hockey.

"I had to stop working because of my health issues, so I was very isolated," she said.

Since volunteering at Belong in Hockey, Ms Gilbar has been able to build up her strength and return to the sport.

"Being able to come out here just gave me that social connection," she said.

"It gave me hockey back."

World.title: Whistleblower's plea to remove gag orders ahead of landmark ADF sexual violence inquiry
World.content:
The first hearings as part of a landmark inquiry into military sexual violence could be mere weeks away, but advocates in the space fear it will be "half-baked", unless the Department of Defence lifts gag orders.

The Human Rights Law Centre, charities and campaigners have penned a letter to the Chief of Defence and multiple federal government ministers, urging them to provide permanent amnesty to victims of sexual violence who are bound by non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) so they can participate in the inquiry.

"This is a real opportunity in Australia now to reckon with sexual violence, especially in the military," said Regina Featherstone, a senior lawyer at the Human Rights Law Centre.

The inquiry into military sexual violence was a recommendation from the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide. (ABC News)

"We see [NDAs] as a huge barrier to truth-telling and the purpose of the inquiry.

"There's a huge cohort lost, a huge opportunity lost, if we don't hear from [some of those worst affected]."

The letter, sighted by the ABC, urges Defence and the government to release a statement asserting they wouldn't seek to enforce confidentiality and non-disparagement terms against current and former personnel who wish to provide testimony to the inquiry.

The inquiry into military sexual violence was a recommendation of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, which heard disturbing accounts of sexual assault and inaction within ranks.

The final terms of reference for that inquiry are still in development, ahead of hearings which the ABC has been told are on track to commence at the beginning of the new financial year.

Ex-servicewoman gagged for 15 years

One of the signatories on the letter is former servicewoman Julia Delaforce, who was gagged for 15 years.

In 2010, Ms Delaforce said she was trapped in a room, held at knifepoint and threatened with a machete by an intoxicated corporal, who demanded she give him oral sex.

"I kept thinking he may have had a [pistol] … behind his desk," Ms Delaforce said.

" And when he pulled out the machete, I actually for a second felt relief, because I thought, I can fight a machete. I can't fight a pistol; I'll be dead. "

Julia Delaforce says she was threatened by an intoxicated corporal in 2010. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

When she managed to flee the room, Ms Delaforce said her bosses told her to go back in, calm down her attacker and drive him home.

"I was the only woman present, and I was the lowest ranking member, and I was a reservist," Ms Delaforce said.

Frustrated with a lack of action from her higher-ups after the incident, Ms Delaforce lodged a complaint with the Human Rights Commission.

Three years later, the matter was settled, but the caveat was that Ms Delaforce had to sign her voice away through an NDA.

Ms Delaforce said at the time, she was "sick" with the effects of post-traumatic stress disorder, and the smallest of things could trigger a breakdown.

Ms Delaforce ended up signing an NDA, and dealt with post-traumatic stress disorder following the incident. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"I was constantly looking for concealed weapons," she said.

Defence support services: The Defence all-hours Support Line is a confidential telephone and online service for ADF members and their families 1800 628 036

Open Arms provides 24-hour free and confidential counselling and support for current and former ADF members and their families 1800 011 046

Soldier On is a national support services provider for Defence personnel, contemporary veterans, and their families. Contact during office hours 1300 620 380

"Even on regular people like my husband, he might just be buttering bread or making dinner and chopping carrots or something, and it would set me into a full panic attack."

Ms Delaforce said the NDA prevented her from participating in the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, despite her requesting multiple times to have it waived.

It was then that she turned to Regina Featherstone for help, launching legal action to overturn her NDA.

In 2025, after 15 years living under the NDA, that's exactly what she managed to do.

"I essentially won my voice back," she said.

"It was a landmark moment for me, but also for others silenced by their employers. I felt vindicated and I felt like that weight had been lifted."

Since the court's decision in 2025, Ms Delaforce has started the Ban the NDA campaign, calling for non-disclosure agreements that wish to silence victims of workplace harassment or unlawful conduct to be outlawed.

She wants to see the same rights secured for others, so they can speak up at the inquiry.

Julia Delaforce started the Ban the NDA campaign in 2025. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"It'll be a half-baked [inquiry] if they can't encapsulate the worst-affected people," she said.

"It can't fulfil its purpose, and it'll create structural gaps in evidence and undermine the credibility of the process … if all relevant voices [can't be] heard."

A Defence spokesperson told the ABC that the department does not prevent participants from sharing their experiences.

"Defence is dedicated to preventing sexual violence and acting on incidents sensitively, diligently and in a trauma-informed way," they said.

"Support services are available to current and former Defence personnel at all times.

"There will be no adverse consequences for current or former ADF members, Commonwealth employees or contractors arising from their decision to participate in the inquiry.

"Defence does not prevent a participant from sharing their lived experience with others and supports people when they choose to do so."

A 'case-by-case' review

At a Senate hearing in December, Defence's chief counsel, Francesca Rush, said it was not the organisation's practice to use NDAs and it "does not stop people from trying to tell their stories".

Ms Rush admitted that Defence did not know how many members who had been victims of sexual violence, were bound by NDAs.

The outgoing Chief of the Defence Force, Admiral David Johnston, told the Senate hearing he understood that NDAs could cause "concern" for victims.

Admiral David Johnston is the outgoing Chief of the Australian Defence Force. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"The circumstances of those non-disclosure arrangements, of course, vary widely, particularly to meet the preferences of one of the parties," he said.

"I think we would certainly offer to review each one of them on a case-by-case basis, were any of the parties to raise it with us and ask for a reconsideration of the terms of the NDA."

Ms Featherstone believes the upcoming inquiry is a time for Defence to listen and act.

"I don't think it's had that chance before … because it operated ... with a culture of silence," she said.

"And now, we do — if we remove these barriers to truth-telling."

World.title: Whale disposal scrutinised after boat ramp 'debacle' attracts sharks
World.content:
Experts are calling for an overhaul of dead whale disposals after the removal of a carcass at a boat ramp north of Wollongong attracted more than a dozen sharks and angered locals.

The carcass was pulled from a rock shelf at Era Beach in the Royal National Park and towed to Wollongong's Bellambi Boat Ramp, where it was hauled from the water by an excavator and taken to landfill.

Divers, surfers and swimmers say they were put in danger by the removal because no safety warnings were issued, and the operation attracted at least 16 sharks to the area.

The operation to remove the whale left the water around the Bellambi Boat Ramp churned and bloodied. (Supplied: Ben Shaw)

It was labelled a "debacle" by Greens MLC Cate Faerhmann in parliament this week, and Wollongong mayor Tania Brown said "mistakes were made".

Dr Olaf Meynecke has studied whale disposal for Griffith University's Whales and Climate Research Program and said with the whale population growing and the migration season approaching, the processes need to be reviewed.

"We're definitely looking at higher numbers and the population is adapting to changes in the environment which means sometimes carcasses show up in places where they have never been seen before," he said.

Local man Jake Oliver captured this drone image of a shark near the boat ramp on Saturday. (Supplied: Jake Oliver)

Offshore disposal

Dr Meynecke wants to see whales disposed offshore rather than dumped in landfill or buried.

"Towing whales offshore has been proven as an effective method," he said.

" We've got the tools on hand. We can predict where the carcasses are going and they're fitted with GPS trackers, so we know exactly where they are at any one moment in time. "

Dr Meynecke said as part of his research, he successfully tracked a whale carcass towed offshore by a Queensland council in 2023 until it sank, and he is now trialling the method with other authorities successfully.

The NSW National Parks and Wildlife oversaw last week's removal to Bellambi and area manager Brendon Neilly previously said the carcass could not be towed out because of a potential shipping hazard.

The ABC understands the department's management plan does not include offshore towing because a previous attempt they undertook was unsuccessful with the whale carcass washing back into shore.

Dr Meynecke successfully monitored the towing of a whale offshore by a Queensland council in 2023. (Supplied: Paddy Marine)

Dr Meynecke said while they need more case studies, by tracking current forecasts and towing carcasses far enough, they can avoid that.

"This is a viable method that's cost-effective and is also returning the nutrients back to the sea," he said.

It's something marine biologist with Humane World for Animals Lawrence Chlebeck also wants to see.

"There needs to be a much better way — a standard procedure for handling," he said.

" Every situation is going to be different, but it's probably safest for the carcass to be dragged as far out to sea as feasibly possible. "

Who is responsible?

Dr Meynecke said a centralised agency on whale disposal led by the state government should also be established to take pressure off local councils, and to create a unified management plan.

He said it should include local Aboriginal communities — for whom whales hold cultural significance — as well as scientists and state and local council authorities.

Currently the land manager of the area where a carcass is stranded is responsible for disposal, which in most cases are local councils.

Last week's removal was overseen by NPWS because the whale washed into Era Beach, but the jurisdictions created confusion.

Tania Brown says the process needs to be reviewed. (ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt)

The department said that, as the landowner, Wollongong City Council should have issued safety warnings for beaches and the ocean in their region.

Wollongong Mayor Tania Brown said that was not made clear.

"The communications from National Parks was that it was their operation and the email was not for distribution," she said.

" We need to work better with the state government on how we manage all of these. "

In a statement, NPWS said they had committed to an all-agency review which would look at "responsibilities, coordination, public safety and communication".

Councillor Brown said Wollongong council supported a new centralised approach.

Local man Darren Bissett captured this photo of the whale being towed in water he had been diving in. (Supplied: Darren Bissett)

"I think we need to look at all options that would do it much better than was done the other day," she said.

"It needs a coordinated approach [and] National Parks and Wildlife should be leading that so that all councils can learn from this."

World.title: The invisible problem sitting under Queensland streets and homes
World.content:
When a large water main burst and began to flood Kristy Reid-Smith's north Brisbane home, the first sign of trouble hit her on the toes.

"I was sitting cross-legged on my work chair and went to put my foot down on the floor and I was like, 'oh, it's a little bit wet'. I looked down and I just saw this water rushing underneath the wall," Ms Reid-Smith said.

The water gushed through their property for about two hours and inundated the bottom storey of their home.

"There was just this torrent of water that was coming through the house … inside, I think it was about two, three inches deep … and then around the sides of the house it got just below knee height," Ms Reid-Smith said.

"The water was so strong that we had a steel frame pool around the side of the house, it buckled the frame of the pool and actually pushed it about 50 to 100 metres up the street," she said.

Kristy Reid-Smith and her family have had to temporarily move out of their home. (ABC News: Hannah Moon)

Ms Reid-Smith said the disruption had meant "massive adjustments" for her young family.

"It's been pretty full-on … on a moment's notice we had to pack up and move out," she said.

A spokesperson for Urban Utilities, which manages this area of the network, said they have crews on stand-by 24/7 to respond to network incidents.

"We recognise there are instances where members of the community are impacted by these incidents, and we apologise for this," they said.

Urban Utilities says factors like changing weather conditions, ground movement and soil conditions could cause a pipe to age at different rates. (Supplied)

A symptom of a bigger problem

Beneath Brisbane's streets, a network of pipes laid as far back as the 1890s continues to provide water to the public. It's part of a large cohort of ageing water infrastructure across Queensland.

At least 22,000km of water mains in Queensland's network are headed towards the end of their useful lifespan. The Queensland Water Regional Alliance (QWRAP) has dubbed the situation the "infrastructure cliff".

A significant amount of Queensland's pipe network was built in the infrastructure boom following World War II, with a large cohort of asbestos cement (AC) water mains installed between the 1960s and 90s.

Kirsty Reid-Smith says there were several inches of water inside her house after a large water main burst. (Supplied)

Those AC pipes are expected to reach the end of their useful life from 2030 onwards.

Exacerbating the risk is the fact that a large percentage of Queensland's newer pipes are projected to reach their end-of-life period during the peak of AC replacement.

Modelling from QWRAP's 2018 Infrastructure Cliff Report suggested if "business as usual practices" continued, Queensland would experience an acceleration in pipe bursts and breaks as the network continued to age.

Local Government Authorities Queensland has been tasked with updating QWRAP's 2018 Infrastructure Cliff report. The updated report is expected in the coming months.

Inside Queensland's water supply

In south-east Queensland, water distributor-retailers, like Urban Utilities and Unity Water, operate as for-profit statutory authorities, owned by stakeholder councils.

It means they primarily source funding for future maintenance through their customer base.

Water management and distribution models differ depending on location. (ABC News: Peter Mullins)

Outside of the south-east, the system is usually more direct, with local councils often managing the entire process from the source to customers' taps.

The Queensland Water Directorate is the central industry advisory body for urban water in Queensland. Chief executive Georgina Davis said the lack of funding was a major barrier to proactive maintenance for councils managing their own water supply.

Georgina Davis says there has not been enough funding to support renewal and replacement of ageing water assets. (Supplied)

"Funding to local government for urban water ceased in 2009 and there has been no dedicated, ongoing funding program from state or federal government to support … the renewal and replacement of ageing water assets," she said.

Dr Davis said more support was needed, with the estimated cost to replace in-ground assets in areas "conservatively as high as $1.8 billion by 2030 and $3.8 billion by 2040."

A spokesperson for local government and water minister, Ann Leahy, said water infrastructure has been neglected in the past.

"The Crisafulli Government is investing billions of dollars to support Queensland council's deliver residential water infrastructure," the spokesperson said.

David Brooker says some of Brisbane's pipe network was laid in the 1890s. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

David Brooker, from Urban Utilities, said 9 per cent of Urban Utilities' network was planned, designed and built when the technology of the day was horse and carriage on the streets of Brisbane. He said many of those pipes were still working as they should.

"We use a risk-based approach to assess where that pipe is sitting in its life cycle," he said.

" Age is one factor, but it's not a great factor of determining whether or not a pipe is ready to be replaced. "

He said factors like changing weather conditions, ground movement and soil conditions could cause a pipe to age at a different rate.

"What also happens as south-east Queensland grows is that … the streets get more dense and more things get built over the in-ground assets, and so they also impact how we maintain, monitor and renew those assets through a pipe's life cycle," he said.

David Brooker says relining an old pipe can extend its life by 50 years. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

He said because of this, a fair portion of the repairs happened through reactive maintenance.

"We are increasingly installing monitoring to see how assets are performing in real time. We do condition assessment … and then we review and replace pipes," he said.

Mr Brooker said relining sections of ageing pipe can extend their lifespan. That approach, similar to keyhole surgery, minimises the amount of ground that has to be dug up, limiting disruption to customers and speeding up the repair.

A significant amount of Queensland's pipe network was built in the infrastructure boom following World War II. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"We pull this folded pipe through the existing pipe, and then unfold it within the existing pipe and that will then expand out to basically press against the walls of the larger pipe and that will extend the life of … that pipe for another 50 years," he said.

However, pipe bursts are not always predictable, and the impacts of reactive maintenance are being felt by Queensland households.

Water restored after burst water main in Brisbane Water has been restored to hundreds of homes which were left disconnected after two pipes burst in Brisbane's east on Monday.

An active construction zone

Since the pipe burst in February, Ms Reid-Smith and her family have been forced into temporary accommodation while repairs are underway. She told the ABC the works were not expected to be completed until June.

"The house is still an active construction zone. All of the sheets are out of the wall and we can't use our downstairs area at all … there's no laundry," she said.

"It's made the house almost not feel like home anymore, because I'm a little bit nervous and I know it's probably irrational, but I can't help it."

While the family is still dealing with the after-effects of the flooding, Ms Reid-Smith said she was concerned others may face a similar situation as pipes across the state approach breaking point.

World.title: Leah Purcell's The Drover's Wife becomes a powerful new opera
World.content:
The Drover's Wife, Leah Purcell's retelling of Henry Lawson's 1892 short story, is getting the operatic treatment.

The production marks the latest evolution of Purcell's Legend of Molly Johnson, a retelling that frames Lawson's story through feminist and First Nations perspectives.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that the following article contains the name of a person who has died.

The opera is a result of collaboration between Purcell, a Goa, Gunggari, Wakka Wakka Murri woman, and George Palmer, a former judge turned composer.

New Australian operas are quite rare, and this one carries particular weight.

"[The opera] is Australian history, black and white, [combining] two ancient forms of story telling," Purcell says ahead of the opera's premiere at the Queensland Performing Art Centre's new Glasshouse Theatre on May 13.

Leah Purcell has reimagined The Drover's Wife as a play, novel, film, and now an opera. (QPAC: David Kelly)

Purcell has been the face and voice of Molly Johnson, acting in the play and film, as well as narrating the audio book of the novel.

Now she's passing the role to her relative Nina Korbe, a rising force in Australian opera and a familiar voice to ABC Classic listeners.

The collaboration breathes new life into a story about survival, resilience, and the stark historical truths of race and gendered violence in Australia.

An Australian fairytale

Purcell came to know The Drover's Wife as a little girl. Her mum used to read her the story.

"The first time I used my imagination to connect to a story, it wasn't Snow White or Cinderella. It was the Drover's Wife," Purcell says.

Lawson's original Drover's Wife tells the story of an unnamed bush-woman living in a shanty miles away from the nearest town.

Loading Instagram content

With four kids and a dog to look after, she dealt with a snake in a dark stormy night while her husband went a-droving.

It was published numerous times in magazines and Lawson's short story collections.

Living in the outskirts of a Queensland country town, Purcell could relate to the little boy in Lawson's story.

"We had a combustion stove, so we had a wood heap. My mum would split the logs into chips and she'd say to me: 'Don't ever stack the wood heap hollow or snakes will get in under'," Purcell says.

"They're actual words from Henry Lawson."

Purcell wanted her adaptation to reveal the voiceless women of the time and the First Nations people, to "make them the heart of my interpretation."

The snake became a totem of an Aboriginal hero character, Yadaka, based on the story of her and Korbe's common ancestor.

Finding the heart of an Australian story

Palmer comes from a completely different background to Purcell and Korbe.

Born to a British family who migrated to Australia in 1947, his parents told him to "get a real job" rather than pursue music when he left school.

He built a distinguished legal career, rising from lawyer to judge, all while composing privately.

Palmer finally turned to music full time after retiring in 2011.

Composer George Palmer has been seeking stories with distinctly Australian characters during his late‑blooming music career. (Opera Australia: Keith Saunders)

The Drover's Wife is Palmer's second opera, following his adaptation of Tim Winton's Cloudstreet in 2016.

He had been searching for another compelling Australian story ever since.

That search ended, he says, "quite by chance," when he noticed Purcell's novel on his wife's bedside table.

Palmer had already seen Purcell's play in 2016.

Encountering the book a few years later sparked something deeper.

"I had one of these blinding thunderclap moments of: that's the story I have been looking for," Palmer says.

It would be another year before Purcell and her partner, Bain Stewart, met with Palmer to discuss the possibility of an operatic adaptation.

After securing support from the Queensland Performing Arts Centre and Opera Australia, Palmer and Purcell went ahead.

"[Purcell] and I worked very closely together [to transform] the text from the play into a libretto for the opera," Palmer says.

Purcell has never shied away from exposing the domestic and racial violence that could land people before a judge, describing The Drover's Wife as "an Australian western."

But for Palmer, the heart of the story lies elsewhere.

"It is essentially a love story," he says.

Nina Korbe plays Molly Johnson in the titular Drover's Wife, taking over the role from Leah Purcell. (Queensland Performing Arts Centre: David Kelly)

"It is about the protective love a mother has for her children and what that will drive her to do to defend them. It is about the love that grows out of trust between two people, Molly and Yadaka, who start off not only as complete strangers but hostile to each other.

"Molly, you see, has all the prejudices of a white woman of that time towards Black people."

Taking on the mantle of being Molly

After a decade of embodying Molly Johnson, Purcell is passing the mantle to her relative, Nina Korbe.

"My grandfather and [Korbe's] great‑grandfather are brothers," Purcell explains.

Both women are descendants of Tippo Charlie Chambers, whose life helped inspire the character of Yadaka.

When Korbe joined the opera cast during its development, Purcell told her: "This is your Molly. It's your opportunity to find who she is to you."

Purcell says Korbe brings "her own strength, her sensitivity, her interpretation to the role," adding that "stories are meant to grow beyond one person."

Korbe approaches that responsibility with care.

"There are family truths that are woven within this story," she says.

In the opera, Molly Johnson is initially hostile toward Yadaka, an Aboriginal man falsely accused of a crime. (Opera Australia: Keith Saunders)

Unlike traditional opera, audiences won't see corsets, wigs or jewels.

"The story doesn't lend itself to that," Korbe says.

"It's not glamorous, but [the costumes and sets] will reflect the raw majesty of the Australian landscape, which is vast, harsh, but full of colours."

Although this is Purcell's first foray into opera, she says it's another form of "doing corroboree for our mob."

"We're sharing a past, but we're also sharing it to heal and to grow."

The Drover's Wife makes clear that the dream of equality and justice belongs to everyone, regardless of their skin colour, even as access to it has long depended on the circumstances of one's birth.

"It's been 10 years since the play, but we're still looking for that equality in First Nations people and violence against women," Purcell says.

With a children's book and TV series in development, Purcell is far from finished telling the story of The Drover's Wife:

" There's still story and life in Molly Johnson yet. "

The Drover's Wife will be performed at the Queensland Performing Arts Centre from May 13–22 and at the Sydney Opera House August 7–15.
